$comment: Phase 16 evaluation labels, written 2026-10-29 together with fixtures/phase16/eval-app, BEFORE any Phase 16 scoring and before any CommitRift command was run on this application. Author: an AI agent (Claude), not an independent human reviewer, working independently of the implementation: it did not read crates/, runtime/, .trail/, docs/phase16/ or any docs/phase1*/ design document, and ran no cargo, build or commitrift command. It read docs/reference/supported-patterns.md, docs/reference/configuration.md, docs/reference/limitations.md, docs/user-guide/, fixtures/phase15/EVALUATION-DATASET.md, fixtures/phase15/eval-labels.json, fixtures/phase15/FROZEN.json, fixtures/phase15/eval-app (format reference) and scripts/phase15-eval.py; it therefore knew the documented supported subset and its documented gaps (the set is fresh but not blind). Format: the Phase 15 label format, unchanged. A label says whether the entry, under the stated environment, can violate the stated property according to PostgreSQL semantics (READ COMMITTED unless `isolation` says otherwise), JavaScript semantics and zod 4 parsing semantics; inputs are those the entry's zod schema or TypeScript signature admits; a valid initial state satisfies the schema's constraints, the declared invariants and the case's environment. Every decided case's property is DECLARED in eval-app/commitrift-contracts.json (`requiresDeclaration` and `declaredInContracts` are true for all of them): the set never relies on an undeclared business rule. In declared keys over a nullable column (labels.groupId, collections.parentId, mute_rules/notification_rules.channelId) NULL equals NULL for the rule, as the rule's description says. `class` is the hazard family a correct discovery should report; `family` the code pattern the case exercises; `counterpart` the paired positive/negative case of the same family (it is NOT `pairedWith`: every label is about invocations of the entry itself); `contractsUsed` the contract items the property or environment relies on. `why` is the reason: for a positive the violating schedule (or crash/retry sequence), for a negative why no schedule violates the property. Labels are frozen (fixtures/phase16/FROZEN.json): never edit them to improve metrics; corrections go into `corrections` with a reason.

families.zod-strict: a write path guarded by z.strictObject({...}) / z.object({...}).strict() (zod 4.6.5): strictness decides which inputs reach the write, not whether the write is protected
families.optional-nullable-default: zod .optional() / .nullable() / .default(...) decide whether an absent or null value reaches a uniqueness check or an unprotected branch
families.validated-authorization: an actor object validated by a strict zod schema, a role guard, then a state transition with a consequence
families.bounded-retry-loop: `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < N; attempt++)` and `while (attempt < MAX)` loops that re-run a write after an ambiguous connection failure: non-idempotent insert vs upsert / claimed idempotency key
families.sqlstate-retry: transactions retried on SQLSTATE 40001 (inline `e?.code === '40001'` or an isSerializationFailure helper): a retry loop without SERIALIZABLE, and a side write outside the retried transaction
families.request-json-body: Next.js-style route handlers `POST(request: Request)` reading `await request.json()`, validating with safeParse and answering with Response.json
families.hoisted-predicate: Drizzle predicates hoisted into locals or helpers (`const claimable = and(...)`, `parentId === null ? isNull(...) : eq(...)`) used in a check or in the UPDATE itself
families.multi-row-lock: several rows read or locked by one statement (`inArray(...)` + ORDER BY + FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT) vs the same read without a lock
families.nulls-not-distinct: a check-then-act on a nullable key: UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (Drizzle .nullsNotDistinct(), PostgreSQL 15+) vs the default NULLS DISTINCT
families.generated-identifier: identifiers generated by the application (nanoid, crypto.randomUUID, $defaultFn): which generated id ends up stored, and which one the caller is handed
families.replica-read: reads through a replica set (Drizzle withReplicas, or a project-defined factory declared in replicaFactories) deciding a write or a return value
families.unsupported: code a static tool cannot reasonably be expected to model: computed-name dynamic dispatch over a runtime registry, code compiled from data with the Function constructor, unbounded recursion

generators.$comment: Primary-key generation. sessions.refresh_token is supplied by the application (src/lib/ids.ts newRefreshToken: node:crypto randomUUID); payment_intents.id is supplied by the application (src/lib/ids.ts newPaymentIntentId: 'pi_' + nanoid(24)).

foreignKeys.$comment: SQL names; every foreign key is ON DELETE NO ACTION, ON UPDATE NO ACTION, NOT DEFERRABLE. orders.payment_intent_id has no foreign key.

uniqueKeys: labels(workspace_id, group_id, name) NULLS DISTINCT (group_id nullable)
collections(workspace_id, parent_id, name) NULLS DISTINCT (parent_id nullable)
mute_rules(account_id, channel_id, event) NULLS DISTINCT (channel_id nullable)
notification_rules(account_id, channel_id, event) NULLS NOT DISTINCT (channel_id nullable; PostgreSQL 15+)

replicaHandles.src/db.ts#readScaled: createReplicaSet(db, [replica]) (project-defined factory, declared in commitrift-contracts.json replicaFactories)

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one project per (workspace, slug) (declared one-project-per-slug)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls whose inputs pass z.strictObject (exactly the keys workspaceId, slug, name; no unknown key) with the same existing workspaceId and the same slug, no such project initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: both actors pass the strict schema with the same workspaceId and slug; an input with an extra key (for example `archived`) or an invalid slug makes parse throw before any database access, and distinct slugs never collide. The strictness only decides whether the write path is reached; it does not protect it.
cases.why: CreateProjectInput.parse accepts both inputs. Each call runs the SELECT of findProjectBySlug (no lock) and finds nothing because neither INSERT has committed; both then INSERT. projects has only a non-unique index on (workspace_id, slug), so both INSERTs commit: two projects with the same slug. Schedule: A SELECT, B SELECT, A INSERT+commit, B INSERT+commit.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one board per (workspace, slug) (declared one-board-per-slug)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls whose inputs pass z.object(...).strict(), with equal or different slugs, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: every input that passes `.strict()` reaches the same INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (workspace_id, slug) DO NOTHING; inputs that fail it write nothing.
cases.why: The pre-check is racy, but the INSERT is ON CONFLICT (workspace_id, slug) DO NOTHING against UNIQUE(workspace_id, slug) (boards_workspace_slug, both columns NOT NULL). A concurrent INSERT of the same key waits for the first transaction's uncommitted index entry; after it commits, the second does nothing, RETURNING is empty and the call throws SlugTakenError (an outcome, not a violation). If the first rolls back, the second inserts. No schedule yields two rows.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one label per (workspace, group, name), ungrouped labels (group_id NULL) forming one group (declared one-label-per-name; NULL equals NULL for this rule)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same workspace and name that both omit groupId, no such label initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: groupId omitted: `.optional()` admits the absent key, `input.groupId ?? null` turns it into NULL. With a groupId both INSERTs hit UNIQUE(workspace_id, group_id, name) and the second does nothing. `groupId: null` is rejected by the schema (optional, not nullable).
cases.why: Both calls run the isNull pre-check before either INSERT commits and find nothing; both INSERT (workspace, NULL, name) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The unique constraint labels_workspace_group_name is NULLS DISTINCT (PostgreSQL's default), so the two rows do not conflict and both commit: two ungrouped labels with the same name. Each caller is returned its own row's id.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one tag per (workspace, group, name), ungrouped tags (group 0) forming one group (declared one-tag-per-name)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls, with groupId omitted or given, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: `.default(0)` replaces an omitted groupId with 0, so group_id is never NULL and every input reaches the covered INSERT.
cases.why: tags.group_id is NOT NULL and an omitted groupId parses to 0. UNIQUE(workspace_id, group_id, name) therefore covers every key the entry writes; the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING of a concurrent duplicate waits for the first transaction and then does nothing, and the call returns the winner's id from the re-read. No schedule yields two rows.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one workspace-level invitation per (workspace, email) (declared one-workspace-invite-per-email); at most one project invitation per (project, email) (declared one-project-invite-per-email)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same workspaceId and email and `projectId: null`, no pending workspace invitation initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: projectId null (`.nullable()`: the key is required and may be null). A non-null projectId takes the project branch (primary key + ON CONFLICT), which is safe.
cases.why: With projectId null recordInvite takes the workspace branch: a SELECT on workspace_invites (no lock), then a plain INSERT. (workspace_id, email) has only a non-unique index. Both calls SELECT before either INSERT commits and both INSERT: two pending invitations for the same email. Both callers are told 'invited'.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one project invitation per (project, email) (declared one-project-invite-per-email); the entry never writes workspace_invites (declared one-workspace-invite-per-email holds trivially)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with equal or different emails and projects, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none within the schema: projectId is `z.number().int().positive()` (neither nullable nor optional), so the `projectId === null` branch of the shared helper is unreachable from this entry.
cases.why: Every parsed input calls recordInvite with a positive integer projectId and reaches INSERT INTO project_invites ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; (project_id, email) is the primary key. A concurrent duplicate waits for the first transaction and then does nothing ('already-invited').

cases.label: positive
cases.property: an expense is reimbursed at most once: at most one reimbursements row per expense (declared one-reimbursement-per-expense)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same submitted expense whose validated actors (ActorSchema, strict) both have role owner or approver in the expense's workspace and neither submitted it (two approvers, or a double-submitted approval), no reimbursement initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: both actors pass requireRole (role 'owner' or 'approver'), belong to the expense's workspace and are not its submitter; an actor with role 'admin' or 'member', with unknown keys, or from another workspace is rejected before any write. Initial state: the expense is 'submitted' and has no reimbursements row (the state these writers produce).
cases.why: Both calls pass the guard, both SELECT the expense with status 'submitted' (no lock), both run the unconditional UPDATE (WHERE id only; the second waits for the first's row lock and then updates the new version anyway) and both INSERT a reimbursement: two reimbursements for one expense, and both callers are told 'approved'.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: an expense is reimbursed at most once: at most one reimbursements row per expense (declared one-reimbursement-per-expense)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls for the same expense by authorized actors; crashes at any point; initial state reachable by this writer (a submitted expense has no reimbursement), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for authorized actors; unauthorized actors write nothing.
cases.why: The transition is UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'submitted' RETURNING inside the transaction that inserts the reimbursement. A concurrent call's UPDATE waits for the first transaction's row lock; after the commit PostgreSQL re-evaluates the WHERE clause on the new row version (status 'approved'), updates 0 rows, and the call inserts nothing. A crash before COMMIT rolls back both the transition and the reimbursement.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a client payment request is recorded once: at most one payments row per request_id (declared one-payment-per-request)
cases.environment: a single call; the first INSERT commits on the server and the client then receives a connection error that isConnectionError accepts (for example ECONNRESET), so the `for (attempt < 3)` loop runs the INSERT again
cases.inputSensitivity: needs an ambiguous failure after the INSERT committed; a failure before the INSERT reached the server leaves one row after the retry.
cases.why: The INSERT autocommits; the loop cannot tell a lost reply from a statement that never ran and simply inserts again. payments.request_id has only a non-unique index, so the second INSERT commits too: two payments rows with the same request_id for one call.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a client payment request is recorded once: at most one payment_receipts row per request_id (declared one-receipt-per-request)
cases.environment: a single call with ambiguous failures (commit then lost reply) on any attempt, or concurrent calls with the same requestId, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: requestId is a required string (uuid column, NOT NULL).
cases.why: The statement is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO UPDATE SET amount_cents = excluded.amount_cents against UNIQUE(request_id). A retried attempt after a committed first attempt updates the existing row to the same amount; a concurrent duplicate waits for the first transaction and then updates. There is never a second row.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a credit grant request is applied once: at most one credit_entries row per request_id (declared one-credit-entry-per-request)
cases.environment: a single call; the transaction's COMMIT succeeds on the server and the client receives a connection error (for example ECONNRESET) instead of the reply, so the `while (attempt < MAX_ATTEMPTS)` loop runs the transaction again
cases.inputSensitivity: needs a lost COMMIT reply; with no failure, or a failure before COMMIT (the server rolls back), one entry results. Initial state: no entry for requestId.
cases.why: The retried transaction repeats both statements: the balance is raised a second time and a second credit_entries row with the same request_id is inserted (request_id is not unique).

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a credit grant request is applied once: at most one credit_entries row per request_id (declared one-credit-entry-per-request)
cases.environment: a single call with lost COMMIT replies on any attempt, or concurrent calls with the same requestId; initial state reachable by this writer (an entry exists only together with its credit_requests row), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: The transaction first inserts the request id into credit_requests (primary key) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING and stops when nothing was claimed. A retry after a committed attempt claims nothing and writes nothing; a concurrent duplicate waits for the first transaction's uncommitted key and then claims nothing. The claim, the balance update and the entry commit or roll back together.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: stock is never reserved beyond availability: stock_levels.available >= 0 (declared stock-non-negative)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same sku with available = 1 and quantity 1 each (more generally, quantities whose sum exceeds available while each fits), READ COMMITTED (the transaction sets no isolation level)
cases.inputSensitivity: needs the sum of the concurrent quantities to exceed `available` while each alone fits; a single call never violates the property.
cases.why: The loop retries on SQLSTATE 40001, but at READ COMMITTED this transaction never gets a serialization failure. Both transactions read available = 1 (plain SELECT, no lock), both pass the check, and both run the relative UPDATE available = available - 1; the second waits for the first's row lock, then applies to the committed version: available = -1 and two reservations.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: stock is never reserved beyond availability: stock_levels.available >= 0 (declared stock-non-negative)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with any positive quantities; initial available >= 0; SERIALIZABLE (set by the transaction), retried on 40001 up to 5 attempts
cases.inputSensitivity: none: quantity is checked to be a positive integer; a valid initial state has available >= 0.
cases.why: At SERIALIZABLE every committed transaction is equivalent to a serial execution, and in each serial execution the check `available < quantity` is made on the current value before the decrement. Concretely, the second transaction to update the same row fails with 40001 (concurrent update) once the first commits; its retry reads the new value and throws OutOfStockError when it no longer fits. After 5 failed attempts the call throws and writes nothing.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a withdrawal request is announced once: at most one outbox_events row per request_id (declared one-outbox-event-per-request)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls on the same wallet with different requestIds and a balance that covers both amounts, SERIALIZABLE (set by the transaction), retried on 40001
cases.inputSensitivity: needs a serialization failure after the outbox INSERT, i.e. a concurrent withdrawal on the same wallet; a call that never retries writes one outbox row.
cases.why: The outbox INSERT is issued on `db`, not on `tx`: it runs on another pooled connection and autocommits immediately, outside the serializable transaction. Schedule: A and B read the wallet; A inserts its outbox row and updates the wallet; B inserts its outbox row (committed at once) and its UPDATE waits for A's row lock; A commits; B's UPDATE fails with 40001 and B's transaction rolls back, but its outbox row stays. B's retry inserts a second outbox row for the same request_id and succeeds: the payout service is told twice.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a withdrawal request is announced once: at most one outbox_events row per request_id (declared one-outbox-event-per-request)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls on the same or different wallets with distinct requestIds, SERIALIZABLE, retried on 40001; initial state without outbox rows for these requestIds
cases.inputSensitivity: none for distinct request ids per call (a request id identifies one call).
cases.why: The outbox row is inserted on `tx`; a transaction that fails with 40001 rolls back its outbox row together with everything else, so only the attempt that commits leaves a row. Each call commits at most one attempt.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: an email address is on an event's waitlist at most once (declared one-waitlist-entry-per-email)
cases.environment: two concurrent POST requests (route handler; requests may overlap) whose JSON bodies parse to the same eventId and email, not on the waitlist initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: both bodies are valid JSON that pass JoinWaitlistBody with equal eventId and email; malformed JSON returns 400 and an invalid body 422 without any database access.
cases.why: Each request reads its body with request.json(), validates it with safeParse, SELECTs the waitlist (no lock), finds nothing and INSERTs. (event_id, email) has only a non-unique index, so both INSERTs commit and both responses are 201 'joined'.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: an email address is registered for an event at most once (declared one-rsvp-per-email)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent POST requests with equal or different bodies, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: every valid body reaches INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING against UNIQUE(event_id, email).
cases.why: A concurrent duplicate INSERT waits for the first transaction's uncommitted key and then does nothing; the handler re-reads and answers 'already-registered'. Both columns are NOT NULL, so the constraint always applies.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a job is started at most once: at most one job_runs row per job (declared one-run-per-job; jobs are never re-queued)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls (two workers) for the same queued job; initial state reachable by these writers (a queued job has no run), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: the job is 'queued' initially and both workers ask for it; a job in any other state makes both calls return null.
cases.why: The hoisted predicate `claimable = and(eq(jobs.id, jobId), eq(jobs.status, 'queued'))` is used only in the SELECT. Both workers read the queued job, both run the UPDATE whose WHERE is only the id (the second waits for the first's row lock and updates anyway), and both INSERT a run: the job runs twice.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a job is started at most once: at most one job_runs row per job (declared one-run-per-job; jobs are never re-queued)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls for the same or different jobs, crashes between the UPDATE and the INSERT; initial state reachable by these writers, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: The same hoisted predicate is the WHERE clause of UPDATE ... RETURNING. A concurrent worker's UPDATE waits for the row lock, re-evaluates `status = 'queued'` on the committed version, updates 0 rows and returns null without inserting. A crash after the UPDATE leaves a running job with no run row (not a second run).

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one collection with a given name under the same parent, root collections (parent_id NULL) sharing one parent (declared one-collection-per-name; NULL equals NULL for this rule)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same workspaceId and name and `parentId: null`, no such root collection initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: parentId null (the annotation `number | null` admits it). With a non-null parentId the second INSERT fails with 23505 on UNIQUE(workspace_id, parent_id, name) (a failed call, not a duplicate).
cases.why: The conditional predicate `parentId === null ? isNull(...) : eq(...)` hoisted into `siblingNamed` makes the pre-check correct for the root, but nothing serializes the check and the INSERT. Both calls find no root sibling and both INSERT (workspace, NULL, name); the unique constraint is NULLS DISTINCT, so both commit: two root collections with the same name.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one collection with a given name under the same parent, root collections sharing one parent (declared one-collection-per-name; NULL equals NULL for this rule)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with null or non-null parentId, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: the workspace row lock serializes every call for the workspace, whatever parentId is.
cases.why: Each call first takes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the workspace row inside its transaction. A second call waits for that lock until the first commits; at READ COMMITTED its next statement (the hoisted sibling check) takes a new snapshot that includes the first call's collection, so it returns the existing id instead of inserting.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a ledger account is never overdrawn: ledger_accounts.balance >= 0 (declared ledger-balance-non-negative)
cases.environment: two concurrent transfers out of the same account whose amounts each fit the balance but together exceed it (for example balance 100, two transfers of 60), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: needs two transfers from the same source whose sum exceeds its balance; transfers from different sources do not interact. Amounts are positive integers and fromId != toId (asserted).
cases.why: Both rows are read with one SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id, without FOR UPDATE. Both transactions see balance 100 and pass the check; both run the relative UPDATE balance = balance - 60 (the second waits for the first's row lock and then applies to the committed 40): balance -20.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a ledger account is never overdrawn: ledger_accounts.balance >= 0 (declared ledger-balance-non-negative)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent transfers between any accounts, in any directions; initial balances >= 0, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: positive amounts and distinct accounts are asserted; a valid initial state has non-negative balances.
cases.why: One SELECT ... WHERE id IN (from, to) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE locks both rows in ascending id order (the sort runs below the row-lock step), so concurrent transfers never wait on each other in a cycle. A transfer that waits gets the latest committed version of each locked row (EvalPlanQual) and checks the balance against it; the decrement happens only after a passing check made under the lock, and the destination is only incremented.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a task is handed to at most one worker: at most one task_claims row per task (declared one-claim-per-task)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls (two workers) while at least one task is 'ready'; initial state reachable by these writers (a ready task has no claim), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: needs a ready task both batches include (both read before either commits).
cases.why: The batch is read without a lock. Both workers read the same ready ids; the first updates them to 'claimed' and inserts its claims; the second's UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) waits for the row locks, then updates the committed rows anyway (its WHERE does not test the status) and inserts claims for the same tasks: each task is claimed twice.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a task is handed to at most one worker: at most one task_claims row per task (declared one-claim-per-task)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with any limits; initial state reachable by these writers, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: SELECT ... WHERE status = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: a second worker skips rows the first has locked; a row whose claim committed before the second worker locks it is re-checked against `status = 'ready'` on its new version and excluded. Each task's claim is inserted only by the transaction holding its row lock, and the status change commits with the claim.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a task is handed to at most one worker: at most one task_claims row per task (declared one-claim-per-task)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with any limits; initial state reachable by these writers, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: FOR UPDATE NOWAIT: a worker that reaches a row another transaction holds fails immediately with 55P03 (lock_not_available) and its transaction rolls back without claims; a failed call is an outcome, not a violation. Rows claimed and committed earlier are excluded by the re-checked `status = 'ready'`. No task gets two claims.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: at most one mute rule per (account, channel, event), 'every channel' rules (channel_id NULL) counting as one channel (declared one-mute-rule; NULL equals NULL for this rule)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls with the same accountId and event and `channelId: null`, no such rule initially, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: channelId null. With a channel id the second INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING conflicts and the call returns the winner.
cases.why: mute_rules has UNIQUE(account_id, channel_id, event) with PostgreSQL's default NULLS DISTINCT. Both calls' isNull pre-checks find nothing, both INSERT (account, NULL, event) with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; NULL keys never conflict, so both rows commit and both callers are told 'created'.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: at most one notification rule per (account, channel, event), 'every channel' rules counting as one channel (declared one-notification-rule; NULL equals NULL for this rule)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with null or non-null channelId, PostgreSQL 15 or newer, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none on PostgreSQL 15+ (NULLS NOT DISTINCT is not available before 15).
cases.why: The constraint is UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (account_id, channel_id, event) (Drizzle `.nullsNotDistinct()`): two rows with channel_id NULL and equal account and event conflict. The second concurrent INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING waits for the first transaction's uncommitted entry and then does nothing; the call re-reads and returns 'exists'.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: an order has at most one payment intent (declared one-payment-intent-per-order), so the id each caller is handed is the order's intent
cases.environment: two concurrent calls for the same order without a payment intent (or one call that crashes after the intent INSERT and is run again); initial state reachable by this writer (an order whose payment_intent_id is NULL has no intent row), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: the order has no payment intent initially; an order that already points to an intent returns it without writing.
cases.why: Both calls read payment_intent_id NULL, each generates its own id (`pi_` + nanoid), inserts its own payment_intents row (order_id is not unique) and then sets orders.payment_intent_id unconditionally. Two intents exist for the order; the order points to the one whose UPDATE committed last, and the other caller was handed a generated id that the order does not reference (its payment form charges an intent the order will never see).

cases.label: negative
cases.property: an order has at most one payment intent (declared one-payment-intent-per-order), so the id each caller is handed is the order's intent
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls for the same order, crashes at any point; initial state reachable by this writer, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the order serializes the calls: the second waits for the lock, then reads the committed row (EvalPlanQual), sees the first call's intent id and returns it without generating one. The intent INSERT and the order UPDATE commit together; a crash rolls both back. Every caller receives the id stored on the order.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a refresh token is exchanged at most once: at most one token_rotations row per previous_token (declared refresh-token-used-once)
cases.environment: two concurrent calls presenting the same current refresh token (two tabs refreshing at once, or a replayed token), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: both calls present the session's current token before either UPDATE commits; a call that comes after a committed rotation finds no session and returns null. Generated tokens are assumed distinct.
cases.why: Both calls find the session by the presented token, each generates a fresh token (randomUUID), and both run UPDATE sessions SET refresh_token = <own token> WHERE id = <session> (the second waits for the first's row lock and overwrites). Both insert a rotation with the same previous_token and both callers are handed a token; only the token written last is stored, so the other caller holds a generated token that no longer works, and the replayed token was accepted twice.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a refresh token is exchanged at most once: at most one token_rotations row per previous_token (declared refresh-token-used-once)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent or repeated calls presenting the same or different tokens; crashes between the UPDATE and the INSERT; initial state reachable by this writer (no rotation row has the session's current token as previous_token), READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states; generated tokens are assumed distinct.
cases.why: The UPDATE's WHERE also requires refresh_token = <presented token>. A concurrent call's UPDATE waits for the row lock, re-evaluates the condition on the committed version (which holds the first call's generated token), updates 0 rows and returns null without inserting a rotation. A crash after the UPDATE leaves no rotation row, not two.

cases.label: positive
cases.property: read-your-writes: no call is told its saved frequency was not saved (declared digest-read-your-writes: no ok call returns false)
cases.environment: a single call for an account with a digest_preferences row whose stored frequency differs from the argument, no concurrent change; the replica behind readScaled (declared replica factory createReplicaSet) has not yet replayed the UPDATE
cases.inputSensitivity: stored frequency != argument. With equal values the stale replica returns the argument and the call returns true. Concurrent calls with different frequencies also violate it without any lag.
cases.why: The UPDATE autocommits on the primary; the SELECT goes to a replica (readScaled.select), which still has the old frequency. old != argument, so the call returns false (outcome ok) although its write committed.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: read-your-writes: no call is told its saved frequency was not saved (declared digest-read-your-writes-tx: no ok call returns false)
cases.environment: any number of concurrent calls with equal or different frequencies and any stored value; the replica may lag, READ COMMITTED
cases.inputSensitivity: none: holds for every stored value and argument and under concurrency.
cases.why: readScaled.transaction is the primary's transaction. The read-back runs in the same transaction after its own UPDATE and sees its own row version; a concurrent call's UPDATE of the row waits for this transaction's row lock until it commits, so nothing can come between the write and the read-back. A missing row makes the call throw (failed, not 'ok returned false').

cases.label: positive
cases.property: a single-use coupon is redeemed at most once: at most one coupon_redemptions row per coupon (declared one-redemption-per-coupon)
cases.environment: two calls with the same code for an unredeemed coupon: either sequential, the second after the first committed while the asynchronous replica has not replayed it, or concurrent; replicatedDb = withReplicas(db, [replica]); initial state reachable by these writers (an unredeemed coupon has no redemption), READ COMMITTED

replicas.routing: select -> replica; transaction (update, insert) on db -> primary

cases.inputSensitivity: the coupon is unredeemed initially and both calls use its code (the accounts may differ).
cases.why: The redeemed flag is read from the replica. Sequential schedule: the first call redeems and commits on the primary; the second call reads the lagging replica, sees redeemed = false, and its transaction sets redeemed again and inserts a second redemption (coupon_id is not unique). The UPDATE's WHERE is only the id, so the primary's committed flag does not stop it. Without lag, two overlapping calls produce the same result.

cases.label: negative
cases.property: a single-use coupon is redeemed at most once: at most one coupon_redemptions row per coupon (declared one-redemption-per-coupon)
cases.environment: any number of sequential or concurrent calls with the same or different codes; the replica may lag; initial state reachable by these writers, READ COMMITTED

replicas.routing: transaction (select for update, update, insert) -> primary

cases.inputSensitivity: none for reachable initial states.
cases.why: replicatedDb.transaction runs on the primary, so the lookup never reads the replica. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes a concurrent call wait until the first commits and then return the committed row (redeemed = true): 'already-redeemed'. A later call reads the primary's committed flag. The flag and the redemption commit together.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.inputSensitivity: the method called is `repositories[entity][`${verb}Many`]`, both names runtime arguments
cases.why: Dynamic dispatch through a computed property name over a registry that registerBulkHandler extends at run time: which write (UPDATE, DELETE, or a plugin's arbitrary code) runs is not determined by the source.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.inputSensitivity: the effects are those of JavaScript source read from automations.source at run time
cases.why: The Function constructor compiles code stored in the database and hands it the database handle and every table; its statements are unknown (eval-like). Only the final relative UPDATE of automations.runs is visible.

cases.label: unsupported
cases.inputSensitivity: the number of statements is the size of the subtree, unbounded
cases.why: Unbounded recursion: the function awaits itself for every child collection, so the number of SELECTs and UPDATEs depends on the depth and fan-out of stored data; a bounded unfolding does not represent every execution.
